safety.en: Ordinary city running needs care, especially in the awkward old town. On race day, dense crowds hid a rubbish bin that runners in our pace group collided with.

scenery.en: A beautiful old town, river views and major landmarks. I still prefer the sea for a running trip.

surface.en: A fast, flat road-marathon course, with paved riverside paths for easier everyday runs.

access.en: The riverside makes it easy to choose your distance. Narrow streets and tourists interrupt running in the old town.

experience.en: Supporters lined the marathon and brought plenty of energy. The constant crowds and close space may be distracting if you prefer a quieter race.

en.title: Sevilla
en.excerpt: A fast marathon, the Guadalquivir riverside and a warm February trip. Where I ran in Sevilla, and where I would head on an ordinary day.
en.body:
I’m writing this after the [28 October 2026 train collision on the Madrid to Sevilla line](https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/29/spain-train-crash-what-happened-in-the-17-minutes-before-the-collision). I took that route by train when I travelled from Madrid for the Sevilla Marathon, so the news felt particularly close. My thoughts are with everyone affected, especially the families and friends who lost someone.

## A city I came to run a marathon in

I went to Sevilla for the **Zurich Maratón de Sevilla on 18 February 2024**, so most of my impression of running here comes from the marathon. And as a marathon destination, it is very easy to recommend: **a fast, flat course that felt ideal for racing**. I can see why so many runners want a place.

I also ran around the city before race day, while the roads were still open. Sevilla is a lovely place to explore, with the **Guadalquivir** running through it and a beautiful old town. It was already warm on that February trip. I remember daytime temperatures of around **25°C in Sevilla**, while Madrid had been closer to **15°C** at the same time.

## Where my marathon route went

My GPX recording adds up to about **42.3 km**. The official marathon distance is **42.195 km**; the small difference is from the recorded GPS line. The map below follows my 2024 run.

The earlier part of the route stayed close to the river, passing **Torre del Oro** and the **Maestranza** area before heading north towards **Puente de la Barqueta**. From there, it crossed over to **La Cartuja**, continued near **Torre Sevilla** and went through the **Triana** side of the city. Crossing back near **Puente de los Remedios** brought the course towards the eastern bank again.

It was much more than a riverside run, though. The middle of the race took in longer city avenues, including the **Santa Justa** station area, before heading south towards **Benito Villamarín**, Real Betis’s stadium. Later came **Parque de María Luisa** and **Plaza de España**, followed by the **Macarena** area and **Alameda de Hércules**. The final city section passed through the centre near the **cathedral and Giralda** before returning towards the park and river.

That is one of the good things about seeing Sevilla through 42K: you get the river, residential streets, wide avenues and some of the city’s best-known sights in one outing. Of course, the road closures make a huge difference. A marathon course through the centre does not automatically make an equally relaxed everyday training route.

![Runners racing on a closed city street at the Sevilla Marathon](/assets/uploads/seville-marathon/seville-marathon-2020.jpg "A scene from the 2020 Sevilla Marathon, used to illustrate the race.")

Photo: [Anual / Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Wmarat%C3%B3n_sevilla_2020An001.jpg), [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0). Resized by Wikimedia Commons.

## Crowds and a hidden obstacle

There were supporters everywhere during the marathon. It felt as though the whole course was lined with people, which brought a lot of energy, but also meant some sections were very crowded. That constant noise and closeness might be distracting if you prefer more space or a quieter race.

In one section, spectators moved aside as our marathon pace group came through, and a large rubbish bin suddenly appeared in front of us. I heard runners hit it more than once as the group went past at race pace. It is something I would mention alongside the fast course: closed roads did not mean there were no unexpected obstacles, especially where the crowd narrowed the space.

## For an ordinary run, I would head to the river

The old town is beautiful, but **narrow streets and tourists make it awkward for continuous running**. I would enjoy that part at walking pace and save the steady jogging for the riverside paths.

The paved path along the Guadalquivir is the part I would choose for a normal run. You have the river beside you and much more room to settle into a rhythm than in the old town. You can simply choose a section, turn around when it suits you and run back.

## Would I go back just for the running?

I tend to prefer running by the sea, and **Sevilla is inland**. Purely as a place to travel for everyday running, it would not be my first choice. The river is a very good substitute while you are there, though, and the city gives you plenty to enjoy outside your runs.

**For the marathon, I would absolutely recommend it.** The course was fast and comfortable to run, and that is the main reason I would put Sevilla on a running-trip shortlist. If you are considering it, check the [official marathon website](https://www.zurichmaratonsevilla.es/) for the current course and entry information.

## Free run clubs in Sevilla

I have not joined these clubs myself yet. These are options based on published information, so check the organiser’s current schedule and meeting point before heading out.

### NORUSH Running Club

A relaxed riverside social run with three pace groups and a social catch-up afterwards. The **Tuesday social run is free**, meeting at **Torre del Oro at 20:30**, with no registration needed; their separate track and fitness sessions are paid.

[Website and schedule](https://norush.club/) · [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/norush.running/)

### OYSHO Running Club Sevilla

OYSHO’s [free community sessions](https://www.oysho.com/es/help/categories/oysho-community) include coached running for different levels. The Sevilla group meets on **Thursday evenings**; reserve a place through the [official calendar](https://www.oysho.com/es/community/page/running-clubs) and use that week’s listing for the exact time and meeting point.

**Know a club I should add, or spotted something that should be changed or removed?** Send me a message on [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/markuskaljuste/) or [Strava](https://strava.app.link/W1a7SCITG7b), and help me keep this useful.
